title: Collections.synchronizedMap: wrapping HashMap + safe iteration
keyPoints: Collections.synchronizedMap wraps any Map with a single mutex that synchronizes every method
Iteration is NOT automatically synchronized; you must wrap the entire loop in synchronized(map)
Compound operations like check-then-act (containsKey + put) are not atomic and still have race conditions
ConcurrentHashMap is superior: finer-grained locking, lock-free reads, atomic compound operations, and safe iteration
synchronizedMap locks the entire map during iteration, blocking all other threads for the duration of the scan
Use synchronizedMap only for quick migration of legacy code; use ConcurrentHashMap for all new multi-threaded code

s1_definition.oneliner: Collections.synchronizedMap wraps a HashMap with a single mutex that synchronizes every operation, but iteration still requires manual external synchronization and compound operations are not atomic.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Single mutex**: every method (get, put, remove, size, containsKey) acquires the same lock object
- **Iteration not synchronized**: the iterator is fail-fast; you must wrap iteration in `synchronized(map)` to prevent CME from concurrent modifications
- **Compound operations not atomic**: `containsKey` + `put` is two separate locked operations with a gap between them
- **Performance**: single lock creates a bottleneck; ConcurrentHashMap's per-bucket locking is 4-10x faster under contention
- **When to use**: only for quick thread-safe wrapping of existing HashMap code; prefer ConcurrentHashMap for new code
s1_definition.analogy: synchronizedMap is like putting one padlock on an entire filing cabinet. Any operation requires the padlock – safe for single operations. But reading through every folder (iteration) means holding the padlock the entire time – nobody else can read or write until the scan is complete. ConcurrentHashMap is like individual locks per drawer – you can scan drawers while others read and write different drawers.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap

  synchronizedMap (single lock):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ get("A")  → LOCK map → read → UNLOCK│
  │ put("B")  → LOCK map → write→ UNLOCK│
  │ size()    → LOCK map → read → UNLOCK│
  │ iteration → must LOCK entire scan   │
  │ All threads serialize on ONE lock   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  ConcurrentHashMap (per-bucket):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ get("A")  → volatile read (NO lock) │
  │ put("B")  → lock bucket(B) only     │
  │ size()    → approximate (no lock)   │
  │ iteration → weakly consistent (safe)│
  │ Threads proceed in parallel          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Collections.synchronizedMap is the simplest way to make a HashMap thread-safe, but it is also the crudest. Every operation – even get and size – acquires the same global lock. Iteration requires you to hold this lock for the entire scan, blocking all other threads. And compound operations like check-then-act still have race conditions between the two calls.

ConcurrentHashMap is superior in every dimension: reads require no locking, writes lock only the specific bucket, iteration is safe without external synchronization, and compound operations are atomic. The only reason to use synchronizedMap is for a quick migration of existing HashMap code when you need thread safety immediately and cannot refactor to ConcurrentHashMap.

In the National Bank of India's EOD batch process, the balance cache used synchronizedMap. During the report generation scan (iterating 200K entries), the entire map was locked for 3 seconds, blocking all real-time balance lookups. Switching to ConcurrentHashMap eliminated the blocking – the scan ran alongside live reads without interference.

Remember one sentence: synchronizedMap wraps a single lock around every operation, but iteration and compound operations still need manual synchronization – use ConcurrentHashMap instead.
